name: Tea country
tagline: Sleep among the bushes that make the tea
summary: Darjeeling's tea grows on about 87 gardens on slopes from roughly 600 to 2,000 m. Stay in a garden homestay, walk the plucking paths at 7 am, watch withering and rolling in the factory and taste the first and second flush side by side.
intro: Darjeeling tea is a protected name: only tea grown on the registered gardens of the Darjeeling hills may carry it, and it was India's first product to receive a Geographical Indication tag, in 2004. Most gardens sit on steep slopes between Kurseong, Mirik, Darjeeling and the Rangeet valley.

You do not need a planter's bungalow to see it. Many garden workers' families run homestays at a fraction of the price, and most factories let visitors in during the plucking season from March to November. Factory visits depend on the day's work: check current status before you travel.

name: Toy train
tagline: Two-foot gauge, a UNESCO line since 1999
summary: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway climbs from New Jalpaiguri to Darjeeling on track 610 mm wide, with loops and zig-zag reverses instead of tunnels. Ride the full line, the steam joyride to Batasia and Ghoom, or just the Kurseong stretch.
intro: The line opened to Darjeeling in 1881 and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999. It climbs from about 100 m at the plains to 2,258 m at Ghoom, one of the highest railway stations in India, then drops slightly into Darjeeling.
Full-line services, steam joyrides and diesel joyrides change with the season, landslides and track work. Book on the IRCTC site and check current status before you travel.

name: Treks and walks
tagline: From one-hour ridge walks to Sandakphu
summary: The Singalila Ridge to Sandakphu and Phalut, the Goecha La trail from Yuksom, village walks around Lava and Rishyap, and garden paths from Kurseong. Graded by hours and height, with lodges and homestays, not tents, on most routes.
intro: Most treks in this corner of the Himalaya are tea-house or lodge treks: you sleep in trekkers' huts and village homestays, which keeps the cost low and the pack light. The Singalila Ridge needs a licensed guide inside the national park.
We grade every walk by hours, height gained and terrain. Permits, guide rules and entry fees change: check current status before you travel.

name: Homestays
tagline: A room, two meals and a family kitchen
summary: Village homestays in Sillery Gaon, Lepchajagat, Dzongu, Uttarey and the tea gardens, usually with dinner and breakfast included. Cheaper than hotels, warmer in winter and the best way to eat local food.
intro: A homestay in these hills usually means a room in a family house or a cottage in its garden, with home-cooked dinner and breakfast included in the price. Expect squash, local greens, dal, rice, sometimes a chicken curry, and tea at any hour.
Facilities vary. Ask about hot water, heating and the road to the door before you book, especially in winter and the monsoon.

name: Monasteries
tagline: Gompas, morning prayers and butter lamps
summary: Ghoom's Yiga Choeling, Rumtek, Pemayangtse, Tashiding, Lava's Kagyu monastery and Kalimpong's Zang Dhok Palri on Durpin. Visit at prayer time, dress modestly, walk clockwise.
intro: Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills hold some of the oldest Tibetan Buddhist monasteries in India, from the Nyingma gompas of West Sikkim to the Kagyu seat at Rumtek. Most are working monasteries first and sights second.
Entry is often free or a small fee. Photography rules differ inside prayer halls, and some monasteries close to visitors on festival days.

name: Kanchenjunga views
tagline: Where to stand for the world's third-highest peak
summary: Kanchenjunga, 8,586 m, is visible from Tiger Hill, Sandakphu, Pelling, Rinchenpong, Deolo, Lava and dozens of village ridges. Clear mornings come mostly from October to early December and again in March and April.
intro: Kanchenjunga sits on the border of Sikkim and Nepal and is the third-highest mountain on Earth. From the Darjeeling hills its massif fills the northern skyline, and from Sandakphu you can also see Everest, Lhotse and Makalu on a clear day.
Views depend on weather, not on season alone. Plan two dawns in a viewpoint town instead of one, and keep the afternoon for something that does not need a view.

name: Wildlife and birds
summary: One-horned rhinos and elephants in Jaldapara and Gorumara, gaur in Chapramari, red pandas in Singalila and Neora Valley, hornbills at Latpanchar. Parks close in the monsoon, roughly mid-June to mid-September.
intro: Within a day's drive you go from tall grassland at 100 m in the Dooars to rhododendron and bamboo forest above 3,000 m. That range explains the bird list, one of the richest in India for a small area.
Dooars parks close every monsoon and safari booking rules change: check current status before you travel.

name: Family trips
tagline: Short drives, warm rooms, easy walks
summary: Routes with drives under four hours, homestays with family rooms, the toy train, the zoo and the ropeway in Darjeeling, boating at Mirik and jeep safaris in the Dooars.
intro: Children travel better with fewer hotel changes. We keep the main bases to two or three, and we avoid long drives on hairpin roads after lunch.
High passes such as Nathu La and Gurudongmar are hard on small children and older people because of the altitude. We tell you plainly where it is better to skip a stop.

name: Honeymoons on a budget
tagline: A view, a fireplace, fewer moves
summary: A cottage in Lamahatta, a room facing Kanchenjunga in Pelling, two nights in Lachung's apple orchards and a lake morning in Mirik, for less than a beach week.
intro: A good hill honeymoon moves less than a sightseeing tour: three bases, at least two nights in each, and one room with a view you pay a little extra for.
Winter brings the clearest views and the coldest rooms. Ask for a heater or a room with a fireplace, and pack warm clothes.

name: Solo and backpacking
tagline: Shared jeeps, dorms and a daily budget
summary: Shared jeeps from Siliguri, hostels and lodges in Darjeeling and Gangtok, the Singalila trek with a guide, and village buses. Possible on about ₹1,500 to ₹2,500 a day outside the Sikkim permit tours.
intro: The hills are easy for solo travellers: shared jeeps leave from fixed stands when full, and most homestays happily take one guest. Women travelling alone generally report feeling safe; use the usual care at night.
Permit tours to North Sikkim and Nathu La are sold per vehicle, so solo travellers save by joining shared group tours booked in Gangtok.

name: Snow and high passes
tagline: Above 3,500 m, with respect for the height
summary: Tsomgo Lake, Nathu La, Zuluk, Yumthang, Zero Point and Gurudongmar. Snow from about December to April, permits always, and altitude to plan for.
intro: Most high points here are reached by road, which makes them easy to reach and easy to underestimate. Gurudongmar Lake is above 5,000 m and Nathu La above 4,300 m.
Roads close for snow and landslides at short notice, and permit rules differ for Indian and foreign visitors. Check current status before you travel.

name: Food trails
tagline: Momos, thukpa, sel roti and chhurpi
summary: Tibetan, Nepali, Lepcha and Bengali cooking meet in these hills. Eat momos in Darjeeling's lanes, thukpa in Gangtok, sel roti at Tihar, gundruk soup in a village kitchen and hard chhurpi on the trail.
intro: Hill food is cheap, filling and seasonal. Squash shoots, fiddlehead ferns (ningro), nettle soup (sisnu) and fermented greens (gundruk) appear on homestay tables in their season.
Darjeeling also keeps old institutions from the Raj and the Tibetan exile years: bakeries, tea rooms and small family kitchens that have stayed on the same corner for decades.

name: Festivals
tagline: Losar, Dashain, Tihar and Saga Dawa
summary: Tibetan New Year at Ghoom and Rumtek, Dashain and Tihar across the Nepali-speaking hills, Bumchu at Tashiding and Pang Lhabsol in Sikkim. Most follow lunar calendars, so the dates move each year.
intro: The hills celebrate three calendars: Tibetan, Hindu and Gregorian. That means a festival in most months, and mask dances (cham) at the monasteries in winter.
Rooms fill around Durga Puja and Diwali, when much of Bengal heads to the hills. Book early and check current status before you travel.

name: Photography
tagline: Dawn light, mist and old railways
summary: Kanchenjunga at first light, the toy train at Batasia Loop, prayer flags on the Singalila Ridge, mist moving through tea rows and the Zuluk hairpins from Thambi View Point.
intro: The best light here is early: be on your viewpoint 30 minutes before sunrise. Afternoons often cloud over, which is good for tea gardens and forests and bad for peaks.
Drones need permission in India and are banned near many sensitive areas, including the border passes. Check current status before you travel.

name: Long weekends
tagline: Three or four nights from Siliguri
summary: Short trips that start and end at NJP or Bagdogra: Darjeeling and Ghoom, Kalimpong and Lava, Mirik and the tea gardens, Gangtok and Tsomgo, or a Dooars forest weekend.
intro: Most of the hills are three to four hours by road from Siliguri, which makes a long weekend realistic. Keep it to one or two bases; on a three-night trip, a second base costs you half a day.
Leave early on the last day: traffic on the Sevoke road and around Siliguri can add an hour or more.

name: Off-season and monsoon
summary: From June to September prices drop, the tea gardens are greenest and the crowds go home. Expect rain most afternoons, landslides on some roads and closed national parks.
intro: The monsoon is the cheapest time in the hills, with many homestays and hotels cutting rates. It is also the season of the second and monsoon flushes in the tea gardens.
Plan buffer days: landslides can close roads for hours or days. Avoid the high passes and the Dooars parks, which close for the monsoon. Check current status before you travel.
